messages.author: 52a3a839013611a4
messages.subject: Summary.fitted.values results for an LGCP
parts:
Hello all,

I am fitting an LGCP over a 60 month period across several different areal spatial units. I want to test the out of sample fit ability of my model so I set the last 6 months to be NA for each unit and run inla(). I am a bit concerned about the unexpectedly large increase in credible interval width from in sample (tight) to out of sample fit (much much wider). I know that the out of sample variance should be larger, but I was not expecting the credible intervals to increase by as much as they did, so I want to make sure I am interpreting the output from summary.fitted.values correctly before I make any conclusions about the performance of my LGCP. If I set link=1 in control.predictor, that means that the forecasted values are the predicted intensities of the LGCP at each time point and the 0.025 and 0.975 quantile columns make up the posterior predictive credible intervals for these predicted intensities, is that correct?

I am still a bit confused as to whether these mean, sd, quantiles, etc values are derived from the posterior predictive distribution itself or based on samples from the posterior predictive distribution? If some explanation of how these posterior predictive estimates (especially the quantiles) are obtained that would be much appreciated!

Jeffrey Wu

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Summary.fitted.values results for an LGCP
parts:
if you set link=1 it will use the link function for the first family. the
marginal for the fitted values are computed using change of variable from the
linear predictor

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Summary.fitted.values results for an LGCP
parts:
in the case where the 'fitted values' are to close to the boundary, then currently, there is nothing you can do except switching back to the linear predictoror scale.

the issue is the internal representation of a density that do not account for a lower and/or upper bound. I know, this _can_ be done, its just coding, and, it has not been done.

the safe thing to do is to use the linear predictor (not fitted value) scale for the latent, and the 'internal' scale for the hyperparameters,

result$internal.marginals.hyperpar

and you can convert or compute, what you need, from this representation instead of other one.
